claims.claim: The daily goal on your tracker: 10,000 steps (ledger row)
claims.notes: Direct fetch of the cbc.ca URL returned HTTP 403; independent web search corroborated the same Manpo-kei/10,000-step-meter framing but I could not pull a verbatim passage from the cited page itself.

claims.claim: Where the mortality benefit plateaus (older women): ~7,500 steps (ledger row)
claims.source: Lee IM et al., JAMA Internal Medicine (2019)
claims.passage: mortality rates progressively decreased before leveling at approximately 7500 steps/d.
claims.notes: Directly fetched jamanetwork.com fulltext confirms the ~7,500-step plateau.

claims.claim: Peer-reviewed studies behind "10,000" when it launched: 0 (ledger row, gap)
claims.passage: There were no actual studies that had looked at '10,000 steps,' at the time the Yamasa pedometer was developed, I-Min Lee, an epidemiologist at Harvard Medical School, tells Popular Science. 'It was a made-up number in the sense that 10,000 sounds good, it's easy to remember.'
claims.notes: Directly fetched popsci.com confirms the quote and the zero-studies claim verbatim.

claims.claim: In 1965, Yamasa Tokei Keiki released a pedometer called the Manpo-kei after a post-1964-Tokyo-Olympics fitness wave.
claims.notes: Direct fetch of the cited CBC URL failed (403 Forbidden). Independent web search of other outlets covering the same Tudor-Locke research corroborates the 1965/Yamasa/Manpo-kei/Tokyo Olympics facts, but not from the exact cited page.

claims.claim: I-Min Lee quote: "There were no actual studies that had looked at '10,000 steps.'"
claims.source: Popular Science, 'No, you don't need 10,000 steps a day'
claims.passage: There were no actual studies that had looked at '10,000 steps,' at the time the Yamasa pedometer was developed, I-Min Lee, an epidemiologist at Harvard Medical School, tells Popular Science.
claims.notes: Verbatim match confirmed by direct fetch; attribution to a named, quoted, institutionally-affiliated researcher is sound.

claims.claim: Lee's 2019 study in JAMA Internal Medicine tracked roughly 17,000 older women.
claims.source: Lee IM et al., JAMA Internal Medicine (2019)
claims.passage: Of the 16 741 women who met inclusion criteria, the mean (SD) age was 72.0 (5.7) years.
claims.notes: Actual n = 16,741; "roughly 17,000" is a fair rounding, not a misrepresentation.

claims.claim: Mortality risk fell steadily as daily steps rose, then flattened at about 7,500.
claims.source: Lee IM et al., JAMA Internal Medicine (2019)
claims.passage: mortality rates progressively decreased before leveling at approximately 7500 steps/d.

claims.claim: Women who took 7,500 steps had the same mortality risk as women who took 10,000.
claims.source: Lee IM et al., JAMA Internal Medicine (2019)
claims.passage: mortality rates progressively decreased before leveling at approximately 7500 steps/d.
claims.notes: The paper documents a plateau at ~7,500 steps but the fetched text does not explicitly state that 7,500 and 10,000 steps carry identical mortality risk; the exhibit's phrasing is a reasonable but slightly stronger inference than the source states outright.

claims.claim: A 2022 Lancet Public Health meta-analysis of 15 cohorts found the same plateau, roughly 6,000 to 8,000 steps for older adults.
claims.source: Paluch AE et al., The Lancet Public Health (2022)
claims.notes: Direct fetch of thelancet.com (fulltext and PDF) returned 403 both times. Independent web search surfaced text extracted from the same PDF stating a plateau of '6000-8000 steps per day' for adults 60+, which matches the exhibit, but I could not personally retrieve a verbatim passage from the source page.

claims.claim: CARDIA study: participants at ≥7,000 steps had 50-70% lower mortality than those below.
claims.source: Paluch AE et al., JAMA Network Open (2021)
claims.passage: participants taking at least 7000 steps/d, compared with those taking fewer than 7000 steps/d, had a 50% to 70% lower risk of mortality
claims.notes: Verbatim match confirmed by direct fetch of jamanetwork.com.

claims.claim: From there it laundered upward, promoted in the United States by a former Surgeon General in the 1990s.
claims.source: Uncited entry: "Contemporary reporting on the 1990s US promotion of the 10,000 figure by a former Surgeon General." (no URL, no name given)
claims.notes: The listed source has no URL and names no individual; independent search found no primary documentation of a 1990s Surgeon General promotion of the '10,000 steps' figure specifically, and the one well-documented Surgeon General walking initiative ("Step It Up!") dates to 2015, which cuts against the claim as stated.

claims.claim: "Nobody. A brand name is not a claim made under oath, and Yamasa never pretended it was running a clinical trial."
claims.source: Narrator framing, not a sourced factual claim
claims.notes: Complies with the attribution rule (institutional, non-accusatory framing) but is an editorial judgment rather than a claim traceable to a primary source.

claims.claim: "I-Min Lee, a Harvard epidemiologist who studies steps and mortality, put the provenance plainly" (attribution of quote to named individual).
claims.passage: I-Min Lee, an epidemiologist at Harvard Medical School, tells Popular Science.
claims.notes: Named individual is quoted directly by a named outlet with an institutional affiliation; paper trail is sound.
